t: Number of Equal Numbers Blocks — Binary Search Block Boundaries
o: We interact with a gigantic run-length-encoded-style array through at(index) and must count maximal blocks of equal adjacent values. Reading every element is impossible (length up to 1e15). However, each block is a contiguous run, so from the start of a block we can binary search for its right boundary: the predicate 'at(mid) equals the block's value' is monotone (true then false) inside the block's extent.
k: Within a block, equality with the block value is monotone in the index, enabling binary search for the block end.
Each block costs O(log n) queries, and the number of blocks is bounded in practice by the test design (sum of elements ≤ 1e15 keeps block counts manageable).

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search each block boundary
a.i: Start at index 0, read its value, and binary search the largest index whose value equals it (first index where the value differs marks the next block). Jump there and repeat until the array is consumed.
s: i = 0, ans = 0; while i < n: ans++, v = at(i).
Binary search on [i+1, n-1] for the first index with a different value; if none, next = n.
a.t: O(B log n) API calls where B is the number of blocks — each block resolved by one binary search

w: An alternative is exponential (galloping) search from the block start — probe i+1, i+2, i+4, ... until the value changes, then binary search the last stretch; this is faster when blocks are short. Pitfalls: 64-bit indices everywhere (n up to 1e15), and remembering the block containing i might extend past n-1 (clamp to n). Follow-up: minimize worst-case API calls when block lengths follow a known distribution.
